steps: Unstable (shock, ischaemia, pulmonary oedema): emergency synchronised DC cardioversion.
Stable: rate control with a beta-blocker or diltiazem/verapamil (digoxin if HF/hypotension).
Rhythm control (drug/electrical cardioversion) for selected/recent-onset; anticoagulate appropriately around cardioversion.
Anticoagulate per CHA2DS2-VASc (DOAC preferred) for stroke prevention.
Identify/treat triggers — sepsis, thyroid, electrolytes, alcohol, ischaemia.

drugRefs.dose: 25–100 mg orally twice daily (or IV 2.5–5 mg over 2 min, repeat to max 15 mg)
drugRefs.freq: regular; IV titrated for acute control
drugRefs.why: First-line rate control in stable AF; slows AV-nodal conduction. Avoid in decompensated heart failure or hypotension.

drugRefs.dose: 120–360 mg/day orally (or IV 0.25 mg/kg over 2 min)
drugRefs.why: Alternative rate control when beta-blockers are contraindicated. Avoid in HFrEF (as with verapamil).

drugRefs.dose: loading ~500 mcg then 250 mcg at intervals (total ~0.75–1.5 mg/24 h), then 62.5–250 mcg/day
drugRefs.why: Preferred rate-control agent when there is heart failure or hypotension; less effective on exertional rates. Adjust for renal function.

drugRefs.dose: 5 mg twice daily (2.5 mg twice daily if ≥2 of: age ≥80, weight ≤60 kg, creatinine ≥133 µmol/L)
drugRefs.why: Stroke prevention guided by CHA2DS2-VASc; DOACs preferred over warfarin except in mechanical valves/moderate–severe mitral stenosis.

refs: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Atrial Fibrillation
2024 ESC Guidelines for the Management of Atrial Fibrillation
ACC/AHA/ACCP/HRS Guideline for the Diagnosis and Management of Atrial Fibrillation

confirm: Irregularly irregular pulse; ECG shows AF/flutter. Assess haemodynamic stability and onset/duration.
disposition: Admit if unstable/new with HF; else outpatient pathway.
